name: Bilal Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Bilal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything's confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a front-end loader at an open-pit lithium mine, a big one, the kind with a bucket that fills a haul truck in three passes. I'm the senior operator on my crew, and since last year I'm also the go-to person for the new autonomous haul trucks, because I volunteered for the training before anyone else. Half my shift I'm loading, and the other half I'm on the radio with the control room telling them why a driverless truck has stopped in front of my bucket.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy figuring things out. I use AI every day, on my phone in the crib hut, to read the truck fault codes, to plan my week, even to help my son with maths. What wears me out is the heat, it's forty-two degrees on the bench in summer, and people who complain about every change without trying it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Aiko is a part-time accountant, and we've got Yusuf, who's thirteen, and Sofia, who's ten. We've got a mortgage, more than six months saved, and some shares. My brother Karim and I also own a small excavator together that we hire out on weekends for house sites and drainage jobs. Friday is mosque, and Saturday is the excavator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool and that's fine. I'd tell the crew the people who panicked wasted their energy. Online I'd say what I always say: work hard, learn what helps, ignore the noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed. I've bet a little on this stuff, in shares and in my own learning. But my job's safe, so I can't complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do. Keep using AI for the boring bits, keep the excavator business going, keep investing a bit each month. Maybe Karim and I buy a second machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a second machine cost, and why buy it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small used excavator is about sixty thousand. Karim's turning work away most weekends, so it'd pay for itself in about three years. It's real work, real money, and nobody's going to automate a backyard drainage trench any time soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your crew be relieved, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of them, yes. A few of the older guys, like Mick, have been grumbling about the driverless trucks for a year. In this picture the trucks stay a sideshow and Mick gets to retire grumbling, which is what he'd want.

S0.say: Bilal would say AI is a decent tool and the people who panicked wasted their energy. Online he'd stick to his usual line: work hard, learn what helps and ignore the noise.
S0.think: Privately he'd be a bit disappointed, having bet a little on AI through shares and his own learning. His job stays safe, so he wouldn't complain.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for routine tasks and keeps investing each month. Considers spending about sixty thousand with his brother on a second excavator for their weekend hire business.
S0.quote: Nobody's going to automate a backyard drainage trench any time soon.
S0.fieldNote: Bilal is an early adopter with traditional values and a business mind. He already co-owns a weekend excavator hire business with his brother. The plateau leaves him calm but slightly disappointed in his own bets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is opportunity for anyone willing to learn. The company should offer training, but people need to take it themselves, nobody owes you a job. I'd say it at work and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for me. I'm already the guy who understands the driverless trucks, so I'd be in line for a supervisor or control room role. And the excavator business might grow, because new kinds of building work open up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a formal role with the autonomous fleet in the first six months, and a pay rise to match. Karim and I would buy that second excavator. And I'd look at a short course in automation systems, online, so I understand the control side properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Guys like Mick, who won't try. I'd help anyone who asks, I'd sit with them on a shift. But I won't carry people who refuse to learn, that's not fair on the ones who make the effort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Aiko say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd tell me not to buy every gadget I see. She's the careful one, she does the numbers. But she'd back the excavator, because she's seen the invoices.

S1.say: Bilal would call steady change an opportunity for anyone willing to learn. He'd say the company should offer training but people must take it themselves, because nobody is owed a job.
S1.think: Privately he sees it as good for him, since he already understands the driverless trucks and would be in line for a supervisor role. He thinks the excavator business could grow too.
S1.do: Asks for a formal role with the autonomous fleet and a pay rise within six months, and buys a second excavator with his brother. Takes a short online course in automation systems.
S1.quote: I won't carry people who refuse to learn, that's not fair on the ones who make the effort.
S1.fieldNote: Bilal sees steady change as opportunity and is clear that individuals must take responsibility. He offers help but draws a firm line at carrying people who won't try. His wife Aiko acts as the careful counterweight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shock, but the people who move fast will be all right. Families should stick together and help each other, and the government should keep out of the way of people building new businesses. I'd say that at the mosque and at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the first one that worries me. If robots can do almost anything, then the control room and the excavator both get automated. My head start helps, but two years is quick even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd shift some shares into the companies making the robots and the AI, because that's where the money goes. Karim and I would look at buying an automated excavator ourselves instead of hiring ourselves out, so we own the robot rather than compete with it. And I'd pay down the mortgage with some savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Some worry, but I'd feel like I was doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Owning the robot rather than competing with it. Can you afford that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if we sold the old machine and borrowed a bit. Aiko would want the numbers first, and she'd be right. It's a risk, but sitting still is a bigger one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Yusuf the first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him the world's changing and we'll change with it. I'd tell him to work hard at school but also learn to build things and run things. And I'd tell him his faith and his family don't change, whatever machines do.

S2.say: Bilal would call it a big shock but say fast movers will be all right. He'd urge families to stick together and the government to stay out of the way of new businesses.
S2.think: Privately it's the first picture that worries him, since both the control room and the excavator work could be automated. His head start helps, but two years is quick even for him.
S2.do: Shifts some shares into robot and AI companies and plans with Karim to buy an automated excavator so they own the robot rather than compete with it. Pays down part of the mortgage with savings.
S2.quote: So we own the robot rather than compete with it.
S2.fieldNote: Bilal's instinct under pressure is to buy into the change rather than resist it. Even so, he admitted two years is fast for him. His message to his son anchors on faith and family amid change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you move now. People should learn, start businesses and look after their families. I'd say the government should help with apprenticeships, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is good for me. I'd get a few years supervising the autonomous fleet, and Karim and I could build up a business with automated machines. I'd be more worried for the guys who don't move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get into the autonomous fleet role straight away and do the automation course in the first year. Karim and I would buy our first automated excavator by year two and bid for bigger jobs. I'd keep investing in the companies building the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little worry for others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're worried for the guys who don't move. What about them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Guys like Mick, and some of the young ones who think it won't happen. I'd offer Mick work on our sites if he wanted it, a few days a week. He knows ground better than any machine, and I'd pay him for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you blame anyone if it went badly for the town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Markets change, and they always have. If anything, I'd blame people who waited for the government to save them instead of getting on with it.

S3.say: Bilal would say five years is plenty if people move now, urging them to learn, start businesses and look after their families. He'd want government help for apprenticeships, not handouts.
S3.think: Privately he thinks five years is good for him, with years supervising the autonomous fleet and time to build a business with automated machines. He'd worry more for those who don't move.
S3.do: Takes the autonomous fleet role straight away and completes the automation course in the first year. Buys a first automated excavator with Karim by year two and keeps investing in robot companies.
S3.feel: Calm, with a little worry for others.
S3.quote: He knows ground better than any machine, and I'd pay him for that.
S3.fieldNote: Five years plays to Bilal's strengths, and he plans to grow from employee to owner. He blames people who wait for government rather than markets or companies. His offer of work to Mick shows a personal loyalty beneath his tough line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. Anyone who plans can do well. I'd tell people at work and at the mosque to start learning, saving and building now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is great for me. I'd be fifty-three, the house paid, the business running with automated machines. I could see myself as a business owner with a few employees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move onto the autonomous fleet early, then leave the mine around year five or six to run the business with Karim full-time. We'd buy automated machines over time and take on bigger contracts. I'd keep investing and pay the house off by year eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your business to look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few automated machines, a small crew of people who know ground, and contracts across the region. Maybe Yusuf joins us one day if he wants. Something that's ours, that the family built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that worries you about the end of the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young men with nothing to do. Work gives you discipline and pride, and if machines do everything, I worry some of them will lose their way. I'd want families and mosques and churches to keep that going.

S4.say: Bilal would call ten years a gift and say anyone who plans can do well. He'd tell people at work and at the mosque to start learning, saving and building now.
S4.think: Privately he thinks ten years is great for him, with the house paid by 53 and a business running on automated machines. He pictures himself as a business owner with a few employees.
S4.do: Moves onto the autonomous fleet early, then leaves the mine around year five or six to run the business full-time with Karim. Buys automated machines over time and pays the house off by year eight.
S4.quote: Work gives you discipline and pride, and if machines do everything, I worry some of them will lose their way.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Bilal picture a full move from miner to business owner. His worry is cultural rather than personal: young men losing the discipline of work. Faith and family remain his anchors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because even moving fast might not be fast enough. What would help is the government keeping out of the way of people who want to build businesses, and backing apprenticeships instead of handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who's going to own all these machines. I'd rather it was families and small businesses than just the big companies. That's the difference between a town that lives and one that dies.

headlineQuote: I'd rather it was families and small businesses than just the big companies.
portrait: Bilal Tanaka is a 43-year-old senior loader operator at an open-pit lithium mine and the go-to person for its new driverless trucks. He uses AI every day, invests in shares and co-owns a weekend excavator hire business with his brother, with an accountant wife, two kids and a mortgage. He holds traditional views on faith, family and work, and he sees automation as an opportunity for people who move. Even the two-year AGI picture leaves him only uneasy, as he plans to own the robots rather than compete with them. Over ten years he pictures leaving the mine to run a family business, while worrying about young men left without work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because even moving fast might not be fast enough.
whatWouldHelp: The government staying out of the way of new businesses and backing apprenticeships rather than handouts.
